newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW-TOCOM to list crude futures in 1999/2000.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-TOCOM to list crude futures in 1999/2000.

text.p: The Tokyo Commodity Exchange (TOCOM) said on Tuesday it plans to list crude futures in the fiscal year starting in April 1999 as its first-ever energy futures contract.

"We hope to secure government approval in fiscal 1998/1999, and to list the contract in the following year," Mitsuhiro Onosato, general manager of TOCOM's planning department, told Reuters in an interview.

Although TOCOM had originally aimed to make gasoline its first energy futures contract, a planned relaxation of foreign exchange controls to be carried out in April 1998 has cleared the way to list dollar-denominated crude oil futures, he said.

Onosato also said oil firms and the government are less opposed to the idea of listing crude futures than oil product futures because they believe product futures would have more impact on the domestic oil industry.
The Petroleum Association of Japan (PAJ), an industry group made up of oil refiners and wholesalers, has maintained a cautious attitude toward the introduction of oil futures.

An official of the Ministry of International trade and Industry's (MITI) agency of natural resources and energy, which oversees Japan's energy industry, said on Monday that it will not endorse a listing of futures contracts unless the domestic companies support the idea.
Onosato said the exchange does not necessarily rule out the possibility of listing both crude and product futures.
"But, in order to attract enough participants to keep the market liquid, it could be best to list one contract at a time, and crude is going to be the first one," he said.

As for types of crude, he reiterated previous comments that Brent blend crude, which is listed on the Singapore International Monetary Exchange (SIMEX) and London's International Petroleum Exchange (IPE), is the strongest candidate.

He said West Texas Intermediate (WTI), which is listed on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX), is not suitable for the Tokyo exchange as WTI prices are largely affected by the supply and demand balance in the U.S. domestic market.
He also said that although a basket of regional crudes could work as an effective price index, it tends to take a while for basket prices to be accepted among traders.

He said there could be some problems to be ironed out before listing Brent on TOCOM as SIMEX currently has exclusive rights to list Brent futures contracts during Asian business hours under an agreement with the IPE.

Onosato said, however, he believes TOCOM should be able to list Brent futures despite the agreement because Tokyo plans to list a contract whose details, such as crude specifications and market holidays, are different from those of the contract traded on IPE and SIMEX.

He also said the launch of Brent futures on TOCOM is not likely to be subject to the agreement as the Tokyo exchange, unlike SIMEX, has no intention of striking a mutual offset agreement with the IPE.
With a mutual offset accord, positions opened on SIMEX can be closed on the IPE and vice versa.
On the liquidity of the proposed crude futures contract, Onosato said that, unlike SIMEX's Brent futures, Tokyo's crude contract is expected to be traded actively as Japan has huge domestic funds.
Abundant domestic funds are necessary for a new futures contract to take off, even though it is intended to attract investment from overseas eventually, he said.
"Especially at the initial stage, the availability of domestic funds is vitally important (for the successful listing of futures contacts). And we have this right here in Japan," he said.
SIMEX's Brent market rarely achieves daily volumes of more than a couple of hundred lots, while IPE trades 40,000 to 50,000 lots each day.
Details of the proposed contract are still being worked out, but the new contract will be cash-settled, rather than leading to delivery of actual crude oil, he added.
